Definition: A unique number issued by the IRD to identify a taxpayer - individual or business - in all tax dealings.
A tax applied to goods and services consumed in Grenada, collected by registered businesses and remitted to the IRD.
A tax on income earned by individuals or businesses, including salaries, business profits, rental income, and other earnings.
A tax based on the ownership of land, buildings, or other real property in Grenada.
A tax charged on certain legal documents and transactions, such as property transfers or agreements.
An official document confirming a taxpayer has no outstanding tax debts, often required for government tenders, loans, work permits, or property transfers.
A form filed with the IRD reporting income, deductions, and tax owed or refunded for a given period.
The IRD's official calculation of how much tax a person or business owes, based on their filed return or available records.
Unpaid tax amounts that are overdue past their original payment deadline.
An additional charge applied for late filing, late payment, or non-compliance with tax rules.
An extra charge added to overdue tax amounts, calculated monthly until the balance is paid.
A formal review by the IRD of a taxpayer's financial records to verify that filed information is accurate.
A formal written disagreement filed by a taxpayer against an IRD tax assessment, within a set statutory deadline.
A specific circumstance where a person, organization, or transaction is legally excused from paying a particular tax.
An allowable expense or amount subtracted from total income before tax is calculated, reducing taxable income.
Tax deducted at the source of certain payments (such as wages or contractor fees) before the recipient receives the funds.
The official date by which a tax return or payment must be submitted to avoid penalties.
An official IRD record showing a taxpayer's payment history, balances, and any outstanding amounts.
Meeting all legal tax obligations - registering, filing on time, and paying the correct amount owed.
The act of submitting collected tax funds (such as GCT collected from customers) to the IRD.
A certificate issued by CAIPO confirming a business is legally registered, required before registering with the IRD.
An individual who owns and operates a business under their own TIN, without forming a separate company.
The 12-month period used for calculating and reporting taxes, which may or may not match the calendar year.
The official document confirming a taxpayer (individual or business) is registered with the IRD.
The IRD's online system where taxpayers can register, file returns, make payments, and manage their account.
A taxpayer's official record with the IRD, tracking their registration, filings, and payment history.
A registration category for legal entities other than a single person, such as companies or partnerships.
A registration category for a sole trader operating a business under their own name/TIN.
A business structure where two or more people share ownership, profits, and tax obligations.
A business formally registered as a separate legal entity, distinct from its owners.
A business that has not been formally incorporated as a separate legal entity, such as a sole trader.
Any organization or individual recognized by law as having rights and obligations, including tax obligations.
The individual(s) who ultimately own or control a business, even if not the registered legal owner.
A person formally permitted (usually via written authorization) to act on a taxpayer's behalf with the IRD.
A formal update to a taxpayer's registered details, such as address, name, or business activity.
The formal process of closing a tax registration, typically after a business ceases operations.
The process of restoring a previously deregistered or inactive tax account.
Total income earned before any deductions or allowances are applied.
Income remaining after allowable deductions and expenses have been subtracted from gross income.
The portion of income that is actually subject to tax after deductions and exemptions.
A business or personal expense that tax rules permit you to deduct from income before calculating tax.
An expense that tax rules do not permit to be deducted when calculating taxable income.
A deduction allowed for the wear and tear (depreciation) of business assets over time.
The reduction in value of an asset over time, often used in calculating capital allowances.
Salary, wages, and other compensation paid to an employee, generally subject to income tax.
Non-cash perks provided by an employer (e.g. a company vehicle) that may be treated as taxable income.
Income that is subject to tax after all applicable deductions and exemptions.
A range of income taxed at a particular rate under a progressive tax system.
A tax system where the rate increases as income increases.
A tax system that applies the same rate to all taxpayers regardless of income level.
A system where the taxpayer calculates and reports their own tax liability, subject to IRD review.
A system where an employer withholds income tax directly from an employee's salary each pay period.
A filing submitted by an employer summarizing wages paid and taxes withheld for employees.
An individual income tax return filed by an employee reporting their income and tax position.
A tax return covering a full tax year, summarizing income, deductions, and tax owed.
Estimated tax paid in advance during the year, based on expected income, and reconciled later.
A projected tax liability calculated before final figures are confirmed, often used for advance payments.
The confirmed tax liability once a return is fully processed and reconciled.
When the same income is taxed by two different jurisdictions.
An agreement between two countries to prevent double taxation and clarify tax obligations for cross-border income.
A status determining which country's tax rules primarily apply to an individual or business.
A person or business not considered a tax resident of Grenada, which can affect their tax treatment.
The origin of earnings (e.g. employment, business, investment), which can affect how it's taxed.
All income earned by a taxpayer globally, which may need to be reported depending on residency rules.
A tax system that generally only taxes income earned within the country's own borders.
GCT paid by a registered business on its own purchases, which may be reclaimed against output tax.
GCT collected by a registered business from its customers on sales of goods or services.
A sale of goods or services that is subject to GCT.
A sale of goods or services that is not subject to GCT at all.
A taxable supply charged GCT at 0%, still counted toward taxable turnover.
A supply taxed at the regular GCT rate.
The minimum level of taxable turnover at which a business must register for GCT.
The periodic filing where a GCT-registered business reports output tax, input tax, and net tax payable.
A mechanism where the buyer, rather than the seller, is responsible for accounting for GCT on a transaction.
The location rules used to determine where a transaction is considered to occur for GCT purposes.
The point at which a transaction is considered to occur for GCT reporting purposes.
An official invoice showing GCT charged, required to support input tax claims.
The portion of a GCT-inclusive price that represents the tax itself, used in calculations.
The amount a GCT-registered business owes after subtracting input tax from output tax.
Relief allowing a business to reclaim GCT already paid on a sale that was never actually collected from the customer.
The value assigned to a property for the purpose of calculating property tax.
The estimated price a property would sell for on the open market.
A tax charged specifically on land ownership, which may be part of or related to property tax.
The assessed value of a property including buildings and other improvements on the land.
The assessed value of land alone, excluding any buildings or improvements.
An official notice from the IRD stating a property's assessed value for tax purposes.
The official register listing assessed property values used for property tax purposes.
A tax that may apply when ownership of real property changes hands.
A legal document transferring ownership of property from one party to another.
A formal legal document, often related to property or contracts, that may require stamping.
A formal legal document (e.g. a contract or deed) that may be subject to stamp tax.
Stamp tax calculated as a percentage of a transaction's value, rather than a flat amount.
A stamp tax charged as a set flat amount, regardless of the transaction's value.
A physical or digital stamp applied to a document to show that stamp tax has been paid.
A method of marking a document to show that the required stamp tax has been paid.
A licensed official authorized to witness and certify the signing of legal documents.
A partial payment made as part of a scheduled payment plan toward a larger tax liability.
A payment method allowing the IRD to automatically withdraw funds from a taxpayer's bank account.
A recurring automatic payment set up by a taxpayer through their bank.
An approved arrangement allowing a taxpayer to pay an outstanding balance in scheduled instalments.
A legal enforcement action allowing seizure of goods/assets to satisfy an unpaid tax debt.
A legal order directing a third party (like an employer or bank) to pay part of a debtor's funds directly to the IRD.
A legal claim against property as security for an unpaid tax debt.
A formal legal order used in the enforcement of unpaid tax debts.
Formal legal steps taken by the IRD to collect unpaid taxes.
Steps taken to recover overdue tax amounts from a non-compliant taxpayer.
An official authorized to enforce legal judgments, including tax debt collection in some cases.
An audit conducted at the taxpayer's place of business rather than at an IRD office.
A review of a taxpayer's filed documents conducted at the IRD office without a site visit.
The IRD's process of evaluating which taxpayers or returns carry higher risk of non-compliance.
A taxpayer proactively informing the IRD of an error or omission before it's discovered independently.
A corrected version of a previously filed tax return.
A revised calculation of tax owed, issued after an original assessment is reviewed or audited.
An assessment the IRD makes using its best available information when a taxpayer fails to file.
An extra tax assessment issued when the IRD determines more tax is owed than originally assessed.
The legal time limit within which the IRD can assess or a taxpayer can claim certain tax matters.
The responsibility to provide evidence supporting a claim - in tax disputes, this often falls on the taxpayer.
The formal written document a taxpayer files to dispute a tax assessment.
The official document from the IRD stating the amount of tax a taxpayer owes.
A formal body that can hear and decide tax disputes beyond the IRD's internal review.
A specific body that may hear appeals against IRD tax decisions, depending on jurisdiction.
The IRD's formal decision on a filed objection or dispute.
An official interpretation issued by the IRD on how tax rules apply to a specific situation.
A formal instruction issued by a government minister that can affect tax policy or administration.
A defined period (often 12 months) used for tax and financial reporting, which may differ from the calendar year.
The timeframe covered by a set of financial statements, used as the basis for tax filings.
Formal records (like balance sheets and profit/loss statements) summarizing a business's financial position.
A financial statement showing a business's assets, liabilities, and equity at a specific point in time.
A financial statement summarizing revenue, expenses, and net profit/loss over a period.
An internal accounting report listing all ledger balances, used to check that debits equal credits.
The master accounting record containing all of a business's financial transactions.
A structured list of all accounts used in a business's accounting system.
The financial records a business is required to keep, supporting its tax filings.
Business profits kept within the company rather than distributed to owners/shareholders.
A distribution of company profits to shareholders, which may have specific tax treatment.
An individual or entity that owns shares in a company.
Compensation paid to a company director, generally treated as taxable income.
A transaction between businesses or individuals with a close relationship, which may receive extra tax scrutiny.
Rules governing how related businesses price transactions between each other, to prevent tax avoidance.
A situation where a company is financed mostly through debt rather than equity, which can affect tax treatment.
Grenada's social security program; contributions are separate from but often processed alongside payroll taxes.
A deduction from pay required by law, such as income tax withholding or NIS contributions.
An employee's total earnings before any deductions.
An employee's take-home earnings after all deductions.
A document given to an employee showing gross pay, deductions, and net pay for a pay period.
A payment made to an employee upon termination of employment, which may have specific tax treatment.
Termination of employment due to a role no longer being needed, which can carry specific pay/tax rules.
A non-wage benefit provided to an employee (e.g. housing, use of a vehicle) that may be taxable.
A daily allowance paid to cover expenses (e.g. travel), which may have specific tax treatment.
A payment made for services where a fee isn't legally required, which may still be taxable income.
Submitting a tax return electronically through an online portal rather than on paper.
Paying taxes electronically, such as through an online portal or bank transfer.
An electronic method of signing a document, which some tax filings may accept in place of a physical signature.
The username and password (or similar) used to access an online tax account.
A security method requiring a second verification step (e.g. a code) beyond just a password.
When an online portal automatically logs a user out after a period of inactivity, for security.
A taxpayer's individual profile on the G-TAX online system.
A confirmation generated after successfully submitting a return or payment online.
A period when an online system is temporarily unavailable, often for maintenance.
The senior official responsible for overseeing the administration of tax laws at the IRD.
An IRD staff member responsible for administering, collecting, or enforcing tax obligations.
A professional (such as an accountant) who assists clients with tax matters.
A person or firm authorized to prepare and file tax returns on behalf of clients.
A legal document authorizing someone else to act on a taxpayer's behalf.
A legal provision protecting the privacy of a taxpayer's financial and personal information.
Rules and practices governing how personal taxpayer information is collected, stored, and used.
The principle/law allowing the public to request access to certain government records.
The official government publication where laws, regulations, and notices are formally published.
A form of legislation made under powers granted by an existing law, often used for detailed tax regulations.
Detailed rules issued to implement and clarify a broader tax law.
A law passed by Parliament, such as the Income Tax Act or GCT Act.
Detailed rules or regulations made under the authority of a primary law/Act.
A formal change made to an existing law or regulation.
The formal cancellation of a law or provision, making it no longer in effect.
A tax charged on goods brought into Grenada from abroad.
A tax collected by Customs on imported (and sometimes exported) goods.
A tax on specific goods, such as alcohol, tobacco, or fuel.
A designated area where normal trade barriers (like tariffs) are reduced or removed.
The Caribbean Community, a regional grouping of Caribbean nations that cooperates on trade and other policy areas.
The Organisation of Eastern Caribbean States, a regional grouping that includes Grenada.
An agreement between countries to share tax-related information to prevent evasion.
The U.S. Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act, which can require reporting of certain foreign-held accounts.
An international standard for the automatic exchange of financial account information between countries.
A limited-time program allowing taxpayers to resolve overdue taxes with reduced penalties.
A short additional window after a deadline during which a filing or payment may still be accepted without penalty.
An official decision to forgive part or all of a penalty, interest, or fee.
A special reduction or exception granted from standard tax rules, often for a specific purpose.
A benefit (such as a reduced rate or exemption) offered to encourage specific economic activity.
A temporary period during which a business is exempt from certain taxes, often to encourage investment.
A partial refund or reduction of tax owed, often tied to a specific qualifying circumstance.
A document issued to reduce the amount owed on a previous invoice, which can affect GCT calculations.
A document issued to increase the amount owed on a previous invoice, which can affect GCT calculations.
Formally removing an amount (like an uncollectible debt) from financial records.
Money owed to a business that is considered unlikely to ever be collected.
An amount set aside in accounts to cover a probable future expense or liability.
A potential financial obligation that depends on the outcome of a future event.
An accounting method recording income/expenses when they're earned/incurred, not when cash changes hands.
An accounting method recording income/expenses only when cash is actually received or paid.
The process of comparing two sets of records (e.g. bank statement vs. books) to ensure they match.
A record of financial transactions organized by account.
A record of a single financial transaction in accounting books.
The gradual write-off of an intangible asset's cost over time, similar in concept to depreciation.
The funds a business has available for day-to-day operations (current assets minus current liabilities).
A measure of how easily a business's assets can be converted to cash to meet obligations, including tax payments.
A business's ability to meet its long-term financial obligations.
A situation where a business or individual cannot pay debts as they come due, which can affect tax collection.
The formal process of winding up a business and settling its debts, including any tax liabilities.
A legal process where an appointed receiver manages a business's assets, often due to financial distress.
A legal status for someone unable to repay debts, which can affect how outstanding taxes are handled.
